Part 1 — Foundations: Aerosol Delivery & Asthma Immunopathogenesis

Aerosol drug delivery

Only about 10-20% of an inhaled dose reaches the lower airways where it can act — the rest is lost to oropharyngeal deposition or exhalation. The sweet spot for lower-airway deposition is a particle size of 2-5 microns: particles larger than this impact in the oropharynx and are swallowed, while particles smaller than this are simply exhaled without depositing.

DeviceHow it worksProsCons
Metered-dose inhaler (MDI)Propellant forces a metered dose of drug out as an aerosol plumePortable, fast, inexpensiveRequires precise coordination of actuation with inhalation; prone to oropharyngeal deposition with poor technique
Spacer / holding chamberAdd-on chamber that slows the plume, allowing larger particles to settle out before inhalationReduces oropharyngeal deposition; forgives imperfect coordinationBulkier, less portable
Dry powder inhaler (DPI)Breath-activated; the patient's own inspiratory effort aerosolizes and disperses the powderNo coordination needed between actuation and inhalationRequires a sufficiently forceful, fast inspiratory flow — a problem in severe obstruction, young children, or the very elderly
Soft mist inhalerMechanically generates a slow-moving, fine liquid mistSlower plume improves deposition versus a standard MDIFewer agents available in this format
NebulizerCompressed air or ultrasonic energy aerosolizes a liquid drug solution over several minutesNo coordination or inspiratory effort required; good for severe exacerbations, young children, the elderly, or altered patientsSlow, less portable, requires a power source/compressor
Clinical pearlParticle size (2-5 microns) is the single fact tying this whole table together — every device is really just a different strategy for getting drug particles into that window and getting them past the oropharynx.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
Why does only about 10-20% of an inhaled aerosolized drug actually reach the lower airways?
AMost of the drug is destroyed by airway pH before it can deposit
BBeta-2 receptors downregulate immediately on first exposure
CParticle size outside the 2-5 micron optimal range leads to oropharyngeal deposition (too large) or exhalation (too small)
DThe drug is metabolized by CYP450 enzymes in the airway epithelium before reaching the alveoli
ENebulizers cannot generate particles smaller than 20 microns
Explanation: Aerosol particles in the 2-5 micron range deposit optimally in the lower airways; particles that are too large impact in the oropharynx and are swallowed, while particles that are too small are simply exhaled without depositing. This is why only 10-20% of an inhaled dose reaches its target, regardless of delivery device.
Exam-style question
A patient repeatedly triggers their metered-dose inhaler (MDI) too quickly and complains the medication seems to "hit the back of my throat." Which add-on device most directly fixes this technique problem?
AA dry powder inhaler (DPI) instead
BA soft mist inhaler instead
CDoubling the dose
DSwitching to a nebulizer only
EA spacer device
Explanation: A spacer (holding chamber) slows the aerosol plume and allows larger particles to settle out before inhalation, reducing oropharyngeal deposition and improving coordination between actuation and inhalation — directly addressing poor MDI technique and pharyngeal deposition.
Exam-style question
Which statement correctly distinguishes dry powder inhalers (DPIs) from metered-dose inhalers (MDIs)?
ADPIs require no patient inspiratory effort, unlike MDIs
BDPIs are breath-activated and require a sufficiently forceful, fast inspiratory effort to disperse the powder, which can be a limitation in patients with severe obstruction
CMDIs cannot be used with a spacer
DDPIs deliver medication as a liquid mist rather than a powder
EMDIs require refrigeration while DPIs do not
Explanation: DPIs rely on the patient's own inspiratory flow to aerosolize and disperse the powder — this is an advantage for coordination (no need to time actuation with inhalation) but a disadvantage in patients with severe airflow obstruction or very young/elderly patients who cannot generate an adequate inspiratory flow rate.
Exam-style question
A nebulizer is generally preferred over an MDI or DPI in which clinical situation?
AA well-controlled outpatient with mild intermittent asthma
BAny patient who wants a more portable option
CA patient who wants to minimize treatment time
DA young child, an elderly patient, or anyone unable to coordinate MDI/DPI technique, or during a severe acute exacerbation
EA patient using inhaled tobramycin cycles
Explanation: Nebulizers require no coordination or forceful inspiratory effort and can deliver higher doses continuously, making them preferable in young children, the elderly, patients too dyspneic/altered to use an MDI/DPI correctly, and during severe acute exacerbations — at the tradeoff of being slower and less portable.

Asthma immunopathogenesis: early vs. late response

Allergen exposure in a sensitized asthmatic produces a characteristic biphasic fall in FEV1:

PhaseTimingMechanism
Early asthmatic responseMinutes after exposureAllergen cross-links IgE already bound to high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells, triggering degranulation of preformed mediators (histamine, tryptase) and rapid synthesis of new mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins) → immediate bronchoconstriction
Late asthmatic responseSeveral hours laterRecruitment and activation of eosinophils, basophils, and neutrophils sustains airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness → a second FEV1 decline
Clinical pearlThis two-phase model is exactly why asthma therapy is two-pronged: a bronchodilator (beta agonist) treats the early, smooth-muscle-driven bronchoconstriction, while an inhaled corticosteroid treats the late-phase cellular inflammation. Treating only the early phase leaves the underlying inflammation — and the risk of exacerbation — untouched.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
In the early-phase asthmatic response, which cell/antibody interaction triggers the initial bronchoconstriction after allergen exposure?
AAllergen cross-links IgE bound to high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells, triggering degranulation of histamine and other preformed mediators
BNeutrophil degranulation triggered by complement activation
CT-regulatory cell suppression of mast cells
DDirect activation of airway smooth muscle by eosinophil major basic protein
EMacrophage phagocytosis of allergen particles
Explanation: In the early asthmatic response, allergen binds and cross-links IgE that is already bound to high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells, triggering degranulation and release of preformed mediators (histamine, tryptase) plus rapid synthesis of newly formed mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins) — producing bronchoconstriction within minutes.
Exam-style question
Compared to the early asthmatic response, the late-phase response is characterized primarily by:
AResolution without any further inflammation
BAn isolated increase in airway smooth muscle mass with no inflammatory component
CRecruitment and activation of eosinophils and other inflammatory cells, producing sustained airway inflammation, hyperresponsiveness, and a second decline in FEV1 several hours later
DA purely neurogenic reflex bronchoconstriction
EComplete replacement of mast cells by neutrophils within minutes
Explanation: The late asthmatic response occurs several hours after allergen exposure and is driven by recruitment of eosinophils, basophils, and neutrophils along with continued mediator release. It produces a second drop in FEV1 and is responsible for the more sustained airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness that ICS therapy specifically targets.

Part 2 — Bronchodilators

Beta-2 adrenergic agonists

Focus drugs (red font): albuterol, salmeterol, formoterol

MOA: stimulate Gs-coupled beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle → activate adenylyl cyclase → increase cAMP → activate protein kinase A (PKA) → lower intracellular calcium → smooth muscle relaxation.

ClassAgentsOnset / durationUse
SABA (short-acting)Albuterol, levalbuterol, pirbuterolRapid onset, short durationRescue therapy for acute bronchospasm in both asthma and COPD
LABA (long-acting)Salmeterol, formoterol (+ COPD-only: indacaterol, arformoterol, olodaterol, vilanterol)Slower onset (except formoterol), long duration (12+ hrs)Maintenance bronchodilation — never as asthma monotherapy (see boxed warning below)

Albuterol isomers: albuterol is dosed as a racemic mixture; the R-isomer is responsible for bronchodilation, while the S-isomer has been implicated in side effects without adding benefit. Levalbuterol is the purified R-isomer, marketed to reduce side effects at an equivalent bronchodilator dose.

Clinical pearlThe SMART study (Salmeterol Multicenter Asthma Research Trial) and related tachyphylaxis data led to the LABA US Boxed Warning: LABA monotherapy is never appropriate in asthma and must always be paired with an ICS. This warning does NOT apply to COPD, where LABA (often with a LAMA) remains a core, unrestricted bronchodilator strategy.

ADRs: tachycardia, tremor, hypokalemia, and (with chronic use) tachyphylaxis.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
What is the mechanism of action of beta-2 adrenergic agonists (e.g., albuterol) in relieving bronchospasm?
AThey block the M3 muscarinic receptor on airway smooth muscle
BThey inhibit 5-lipoxygenase, blocking leukotriene synthesis
CThey bind IgE directly to prevent mast cell degranulation
DThey inhibit phosphodiesterase-4 in neutrophils
EThey stimulate Gs-coupled beta-2 receptors, activating adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A, causing airway smooth muscle relaxation
Explanation: Beta-2 agonists stimulate Gs-coupled beta-2 adrenergic receptors on airway smooth muscle, activating adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP, and activating protein kinase A (PKA) — this cascade lowers intracellular calcium and relaxes airway smooth muscle, producing bronchodilation.
Exam-style question
Why is albuterol dosed as a racemic mixture of R- and S-isomers, and what is the clinical significance of levalbuterol?
AOnly the S-isomer is active; levalbuterol removes the inactive R-isomer
BOnly the R-isomer is responsible for bronchodilation; levalbuterol is the purified R-isomer, intended to reduce S-isomer-related side effects at an equivalent bronchodilator dose
CBoth isomers are equally active and levalbuterol has no clinical rationale
DThe S-isomer is a more potent bronchodilator than the R-isomer
ELevalbuterol is a combination of albuterol and ipratropium
Explanation: The R-isomer of albuterol is responsible for beta-2 agonist activity, while the S-isomer has been proposed to contribute to side effects (and possibly pro-inflammatory effects) without adding bronchodilation. Levalbuterol is the purified R-isomer, marketed with the rationale of reducing side effects at an equivalent bronchodilator effect, though the clinical significance of this difference is debated.
Exam-style question
A patient using a long-acting beta agonist (LABA) as monotherapy for asthma is at increased risk of a serious, potentially fatal outcome — what is the regulatory response to this risk?
ALABAs are contraindicated in COPD
BLABAs require a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity
CNo warning exists; LABA monotherapy is standard of care in asthma
DLABAs carry a US Boxed Warning against use as monotherapy in asthma; they must be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid
ELABAs are only approved for use in children under 5
Explanation: The SMART study and related data showed increased asthma-related deaths with LABA monotherapy, leading to a US Boxed Warning: LABAs must not be used as monotherapy for asthma and should only be used in combination with an inhaled corticosteroid. LABA monotherapy remains appropriate in COPD, where this risk was not demonstrated.

Muscarinic antagonists

Focus drugs (red font): ipratropium bromide, tiotropium, albuterol/ipratropium combination (Combivent)

MOA: block the M3 muscarinic receptor (Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 → intracellular Ca2+ release) on airway smooth muscle, preventing acetylcholine-driven bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion.

AgentClassDosingPrimary use
Ipratropium bromideSAMA (short-acting)Multiple times daily; also combined with albuterol as CombiventCOPD (and adjunct in acute severe asthma exacerbations)
TiotropiumLAMA (long-acting)Once daily — much longer duration of action than ipratropiumMaintenance bronchodilation in COPD (and add-on in severe asthma)
Clinical pearlBoth agents are quaternary amine compounds — poorly absorbed systemically and poor at crossing the blood-brain barrier — which is why they cause minimal systemic anticholinergic effects (dry mouth is the main complaint) despite blocking muscarinic receptors. This is the same structural reason they are given by inhalation rather than orally.

Therapeutic use: foundational in COPD (LAMA is preferred first-line bronchodilator in GOLD Group A); used as add-on therapy in asthma, particularly moderate-severe disease and acute exacerbations. ADRs: dry mouth, minimal systemic effects due to quaternary structure.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
What distinguishes the pharmacologic profile of tiotropium from ipratropium as an inhaled antimuscarinic agent?
ATiotropium has a much longer duration of action, allowing once-daily dosing, versus ipratropium's shorter duration requiring multiple daily doses
BTiotropium is a short-acting agent dosed multiple times daily like ipratropium
CIpratropium is selective for M1 receptors while tiotropium is selective for M3 only
DTiotropium cannot be used in COPD
EIpratropium has a longer half-life than tiotropium
Explanation: Ipratropium is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA) requiring dosing several times daily, while tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) with a much longer duration of action that allows once-daily dosing — both act via M3 (Gq-PLC-IP3-Ca2+ pathway) blockade on airway smooth muscle, but with very different pharmacokinetics.
Exam-style question
Why do inhaled antimuscarinic agents like ipratropium and tiotropium have minimal systemic anticholinergic side effects despite blocking muscarinic receptors?
AThey are metabolized instantly by lung tissue before reaching systemic circulation
BThey selectively spare M3 receptors in the eye and bladder
CThey are quaternary amine compounds, which are poorly absorbed systemically and poorly cross the blood-brain barrier
DThey are co-formulated with an antidote
EThey have no muscarinic receptor affinity outside the lung
Explanation: Ipratropium and tiotropium are quaternary ammonium compounds, which are poorly absorbed across mucosal surfaces and do not readily cross the blood-brain barrier. This limits systemic anticholinergic effects (dry mouth is the most common local effect) compared to what would be expected from a tertiary amine anticholinergic given systemically.

Methylxanthines & PDE4 inhibitor

Focus drug (red font): theophylline

Methylxanthines (theophylline, aminophylline)

MOA: three proposed mechanisms — phosphodiesterase inhibition (raising cAMP/cGMP), adenosine receptor antagonism, and enhanced histone deacetylation (anti-inflammatory). PK: narrow therapeutic index, metabolized via CYP1A2; target plasma concentration 5-10 mg/L. Therapeutic use: add-on bronchodilator therapy when other agents are insufficient.

Clinical pearlThe therapeutic-index numbers are classic testable facts: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, headache, and anxiety often occur once levels reach 15 mg/L; seizures and arrhythmias become possible at higher concentrations still. Targeting 5-10 mg/L is a deliberate safety margin below where most toxicity begins.

Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor — roflumilast

MOA: selective PDE4 inhibition → cAMP accumulation → anti-inflammatory effects, suppressing cytokine release and leukocyte lung infiltration; may attenuate pulmonary remodeling and mucociliary malfunction. Therapeutic use: COPD with severe disease (FEV1 < 50% predicted), frequent exacerbations, and chronic bronchitis — given orally, once daily, primarily to reduce exacerbations (little effect on symptoms/lung function). ADRs: weak overall efficacy due to dose-limiting nausea, diarrhea, and headaches.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
A patient started on oral theophylline develops nausea, anxiety, and headache with a level of 16 mg/L. Why is this drug dosed to a narrow target range of 5-10 mg/L?
ATheophylline has essentially no toxicity at any concentration
BLevels below 5 mg/L cause seizures
CTheophylline toxicity is unrelated to serum concentration
DThe 5-10 mg/L range is chosen purely for cost reasons
ETheophylline has a narrow therapeutic index; levels above 15 mg/L risk seizures and arrhythmias, so targeting 5-10 mg/L balances efficacy against these more severe adverse effects
Explanation: Theophylline (and aminophylline) have a narrow therapeutic index metabolized via CYP1A2. Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, headache, and anxiety often occur once levels reach 15 mg/L, with seizures and arrhythmias possible at higher concentrations — targeting plasma concentrations of 5-10 mg/L largely avoids these adverse effects while retaining benefit as add-on bronchodilator therapy.
Exam-style question
Roflumilast is used in which specific COPD population, and what is its major practical limitation?
AFirst-line therapy for all COPD patients; no significant limitations
BCOPD with severe disease (FEV1 < 50% predicted) and frequent exacerbations/chronic bronchitis; limited by dose-limiting adverse effects such as nausea, diarrhea, and headache
CMild intermittent asthma; limited by QT prolongation
DAcute severe asthma exacerbations; limited by hepatotoxicity
ECOPD with eosinophilic phenotype only; limited by injection-site reactions
Explanation: Roflumilast, a selective PDE4 inhibitor, is reserved for COPD patients with severe disease (FEV1 < 50% predicted), frequent exacerbations, and chronic bronchitis, given orally once daily to reduce exacerbation frequency (with little effect on symptoms or lung function itself). Its use is limited by dose-limiting adverse effects — nausea, diarrhea, and headaches — leading to only weak overall efficacy in practice.

Part 3 — Anti-Inflammatory & Targeted Therapies

Corticosteroids

Focus drugs (red font): budesonide, fluticasone (inhaled); prednisone, methylprednisolone, prednisolone (oral)

MOA: bind glucocorticoid receptors (GR) in the cytoplasm; the drug-GR complex moves to the nucleus and regulates transcription of target genes — inhibiting production of inflammatory cytokines, reducing bronchial hyperreactivity and exacerbation frequency, and inhibiting airway infiltration by lymphocytes, eosinophils, and mast cells. They do not relax airway smooth muscle directly.

Clinical pearlThis is a favorite distinguishing point on exams: corticosteroids treat the underlying inflammation (late-phase response); they are not bronchodilators and will not acutely relieve bronchospasm the way a beta agonist does.

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) — dosing considerations

In asthma, ICS should be initiated in any patient requiring a SABA for symptom control more than twice per week. Available preparations are viewed as roughly equivalent in efficacy but vary considerably in the amount of drug delivered per activation, so dosing must be empirically determined and titrated using low-, medium-, and high-dose ranges from the NHLBI stepwise approach.

ICS are delivered via MDI, breath-actuated MDI, DPI, soft mist inhaler, or nebulizer. A spacer with MDI glucocorticoids and rinsing the mouth after inhalation reduces local adverse effects.

ADRs: dysphonia (~40%) and oral candidiasis (~5%) from local deposition; also HPA axis suppression (low risk except at high dosages), modest bone resorption risk, minor effects on carbohydrate/lipid metabolism, dose-related cataracts and skin thinning/purpura, and a growth-disruption concern at high pediatric doses. Long-term daily oral corticosteroid use is associated with fluid retention, weight gain, osteoporosis, hypertension, peptic ulceration, diabetes, and psychosis.

ICS in COPD

Patients with COPD occasionally respond to corticosteroids, but ICS do not appear to have significant anti-inflammatory effect in COPD — they do not affect disease progression or reduce mortality. They do reduce exacerbation frequency in patients with severe disease (FEV1 < 50% predicted) who have frequent exacerbations, and are recommended in that subgroup.

Systemic corticosteroid therapy

Used for severe asthmatic attacks requiring hospitalization, and sometimes in less-severe acute exacerbations or when patients fail other therapies. For severe asthma (hospital), IV hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone is given, followed by oral doses (prednisone/prednisolone) with gradual tapering. Acute exacerbations are typically treated for 1-2 weeks; longer treatment requires gradual tapering due to HPA axis suppression. Parenteral therapy is also used for some COPD patients and other infiltrative pulmonary disorders.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
What is the mechanism of action of inhaled/oral corticosteroids in asthma and COPD, and what they do NOT do directly?
AThey directly relax airway smooth muscle via a beta-2 receptor-independent pathway
BThey inhibit IgE synthesis as their primary mechanism
CThey act by blocking the M3 muscarinic receptor
DThey bind glucocorticoid receptors, translocate to the nucleus, and alter transcription of inflammatory genes — reducing cytokine production, bronchial hyperreactivity, and airway cell infiltration — but they do not relax airway smooth muscle directly
EThey work by directly inhibiting 5-lipoxygenase
Explanation: Corticosteroids bind glucocorticoid receptors (GR) in the cytoplasm; the drug-GR complex moves to the nucleus and regulates transcription of target genes, reducing production of inflammatory cytokines and inhibiting airway infiltration by lymphocytes, eosinophils, and mast cells. Importantly, they do NOT relax airway smooth muscle directly — that is the job of bronchodilators — which is why steroids treat the underlying inflammation while bronchodilators treat the acute symptom.
Exam-style question
According to national asthma guidelines, when should inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) therapy be initiated?
AIn any patient who requires a SABA for symptom control more than twice per week
BOnly after a patient has failed 3 courses of oral steroids
COnly in patients with an FEV1 below 50% predicted
DOnly in pediatric patients under age 5
EICS should never be combined with a LABA
Explanation: ICS should be initiated in any asthma patient who requires a short-acting beta agonist (SABA) for symptom control more than twice per week. ICS improve symptom severity, tests of airway caliber and bronchial reactivity, exacerbation frequency, and quality of life — but available preparations vary considerably in dose delivered per activation, so dosing must be individualized.
Exam-style question
Which local adverse effects are most common with inhaled corticosteroids, and what simple technique reduces their incidence?
ASystemic hypertension and hyperglycemia, reduced by fasting before each dose
BAnaphylaxis, reduced by pre-medicating with antihistamines
CDysphonia (~40%) and oral candidiasis (~5%) from local drug deposition, reduced by using a spacer and rinsing the mouth after inhalation
DQT prolongation, reduced by baseline ECG monitoring only
EAdrenal crisis, which cannot be reduced by any technique
Explanation: Dysphonia (40%) and oral candidiasis (thrush, 5%) occur due to local deposition of inhaled corticosteroid, particularly with MDIs. Using a spacer device and rinsing the mouth after inhalation reduces oropharyngeal deposition and meaningfully decreases the incidence of both.
Exam-style question
In COPD, do inhaled corticosteroids alter disease progression or mortality, and when are they recommended?
AYes — ICS slow FEV1 decline and reduce mortality in all COPD patients and should be used first-line
BICS are contraindicated in all COPD patients due to pneumonia risk
CICS should be used only in COPD patients with normal eosinophil counts
DICS replace bronchodilators as first-line COPD therapy
ENo — ICS do not appear to significantly affect COPD disease progression or mortality, but they do reduce exacerbations in patients with severe disease (FEV1 < 50%) and frequent exacerbations, where they are recommended
Explanation: Unlike in asthma, corticosteroids do not appear to have significant anti-inflammatory benefit in COPD in terms of altering disease progression or reducing mortality. However, ICS do reduce the number of exacerbations in COPD patients with severe disease (FEV1 < 50% predicted) who have frequent exacerbations, and are recommended in that specific subgroup (often as part of ICS-LAMA-LABA triple therapy).
Exam-style question
A patient is hospitalized for a severe asthma exacerbation and started on IV methylprednisolone. What is the general course of systemic corticosteroid therapy after the acute presentation, and why does it require tapering?
AA single IV dose is given with no further therapy needed
BIV therapy is followed by oral prednisone/prednisolone tapered over 1-2 weeks, because longer courses risk hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression requiring a gradual taper
COral steroids are stopped abruptly regardless of course length
DSystemic steroids are never used for asthma, only inhaled forms
EThe taper is required only to prevent oral candidiasis
Explanation: For severe asthma requiring hospitalization, IV hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone is given initially, followed by oral doses (prednisone or prednisolone) with gradual tapering. Acute exacerbations are typically treated for 1-2 weeks; longer treatment courses require a gradual taper because of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression from exogenous steroid exposure.

Cromolyn compounds & leukotriene inhibitors

Focus drug (red font): montelukast

Cromolyn compounds (cromolyn sodium, nedocromil sodium)

MOA: no direct bronchodilator action — inhibits mast cell degranulation prophylactically; not effective for treating ongoing bronchospasm. Use: mostly historic value; less effective than ICS and largely supplanted by them, though modestly reduces symptom severity/bronchodilator need in young patients with allergic asthma. ADRs: poorly absorbed systemically (inhaled) → little toxicity.

Leukotriene inhibitors (montelukast, zafirlukast, zileuton)

MOA: montelukast and zafirlukast are LTD4-receptor antagonists; zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, reducing leukotriene synthesis. Leukotrienes (LTB4 = potent neutrophil chemoattractant; LTC4/LTD4 = bronchoconstriction, increased bronchial reactivity, mucosal edema, mucus hypersecretion) are important mediators of inflammation and anaphylaxis, synthesized by eosinophils, mast cells, macrophages, and basophils via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway.

Therapeutic use: modestly effective maintenance therapy in asthma (less effective than ICS); used as add-on therapy when ICS alone is inadequate. Also play an important role in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD / Samter's triad) — asthma + chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis + aspirin/NSAID reactions, occurring in ~5-10% of asthma patients (aspirin shifts arachidonic acid metabolism from prostaglandins toward leukotrienes). Leukotriene-modifying agents reduce the response to aspirin challenge and improve overall asthma control in AERD. No role in COPD.

ADRs: dyspepsia most common; liver toxicity noted in some patients (contraindicated in abnormal liver function). Several cases of Churg-Strauss syndrome (systemic vasculitis with worsening asthma, pulmonary infiltrates, eosinophilia) have been associated with zafirlukast and montelukast.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
What is the mechanism of action of cromolyn sodium, and why has its clinical use declined?
AIt is a direct bronchodilator that has been replaced by newer bronchodilators
BIt works by blocking IgE binding to mast cells directly, but is more toxic than omalizumab
CIt is a leukotriene receptor antagonist with a long half-life
DIt has no direct bronchodilator action; it works prophylactically by inhibiting mast cell degranulation, and has been largely supplanted by more effective therapies (particularly ICS)
EIt works by activating beta-2 receptors more selectively than albuterol
Explanation: Cromolyn sodium (and nedocromil) have no direct bronchodilator action — they act prophylactically by inhibiting mast cell degranulation, and are not effective for treating ongoing bronchospasm. Their use today is mostly of historic value, as they are less effective than inhaled corticosteroids and have been largely supplanted by ICS and other therapies, though they retain a niche modestly reducing symptom severity/bronchodilator need in young patients with allergic asthma.
Exam-style question
What is the mechanism of leukotriene inhibitors, and how do montelukast/zafirlukast differ mechanistically from zileuton?
AMontelukast and zafirlukast are leukotriene D4 (LTD4) receptor antagonists; zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, the enzyme needed to synthesize leukotrienes
BMontelukast and zafirlukast are 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors; zileuton is a leukotriene receptor antagonist
CAll three drugs work by inhibiting IgE synthesis
DMontelukast is a corticosteroid analog; zafirlukast and zileuton are beta agonists
EAll three act by blocking the M3 muscarinic receptor
Explanation: Montelukast and zafirlukast are leukotriene D4 (LTD4) receptor antagonists, blocking the effects of leukotrienes at their receptor. Zileuton instead inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, the enzyme in the arachidonic acid pathway required to synthesize leukotrienes in the first place — a different point of intervention in the same inflammatory pathway.
Exam-style question
A patient with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis, and a history of bronchospasm after taking ibuprofen most likely has which condition, and which drug class is specifically useful for it?
AAllergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis; treated with itraconazole, unrelated to leukotrienes
BChurg-Strauss syndrome caused by aspirin; treated with omalizumab
CSamter's triad / aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD); leukotriene-modifying agents are part of management
DCystic fibrosis; treated with CFTR modulators
EPrimary ciliary dyskinesia; treated with azithromycin
Explanation: This triad — asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis, and reactions to aspirin/NSAIDs — defines aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD, also called Samter's triad), occurring in ~5-10% of asthma patients. Aspirin shifts arachidonic acid metabolism away from prostaglandin production toward leukotriene production in these patients, so leukotriene-modifying agents (montelukast, zafirlukast, zileuton) should specifically be part of their management and reduce the response to aspirin challenge.
Exam-style question
Leukotriene inhibitors have been associated with a rare but important adverse effect involving vasculitis, worsening asthma, and eosinophilia. What is this syndrome, and which two agents are most implicated?
ASerotonin syndrome; associated with montelukast and theophylline
BStevens-Johnson syndrome; associated with roflumilast and omalizumab
CSMART-study LABA syndrome; associated with salmeterol and formoterol
DHPA axis suppression; associated with cromolyn and nedocromil
EChurg-Strauss syndrome; associated with zafirlukast and montelukast
Explanation: Several cases of Churg-Strauss syndrome — a systemic vasculitis accompanied by worsening asthma, pulmonary infiltrates, and eosinophilia — have been associated with the use of zafirlukast and montelukast. Leukotriene inhibitors are also contraindicated in patients with abnormal liver function given reports of hepatotoxicity, and dyspepsia is the most common adverse effect overall.

Targeted (monoclonal antibody) therapy

Focus drug (red font): omalizumab

Anti-IgE — omalizumab

MOA: humanized monoclonal antibody directed against IgE; binds IgE and prevents its binding to high-affinity Fc receptors (FcER1, FcER2) on dendritic cells, basophils, mast cells, and other inflammatory cells — blunting both the early and late allergic responses and decreasing free IgE levels/high-affinity IgE receptor number over time.

PK: subcutaneous injection every 2-4 weeks; half-life ~26 days. Therapeutic use: severe asthma with evidence of allergic sensitization — most effective in patients with a history of repeated exacerbations, high corticosteroid requirement, and poor pulmonary function; reduces the most severe exacerbations (reduces hospitalization-requiring exacerbations by 88%). Also FDA-approved for chronic recurrent urticaria and peanut allergy.

Clinical pearlLong-term omalizumab treatment leads to a decrease in both asthma exacerbations AND corticosteroid usage — a 'steroid-sparing' effect that is part of why it is reserved for patients with a high existing steroid burden rather than used broadly.

ADRs: US Boxed Warning for anaphylaxis — bronchospasm, hypotension, syncope, urticaria, and/or angioedema of the throat/tongue, which may occur as early as the first dose or as late as beyond one year of regular therapy. Headache and injection-site reactions occur in >10% of patients.

Anti-IL-5 therapy (benralizumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab)

MOA: mepolizumab and reslizumab are humanized IL-5 monoclonal antibodies; benralizumab targets the IL-5 receptor. IL-5 is the major cytokine responsible for eosinophil growth, differentiation, recruitment, and activation — these drugs inhibit eosinophilic inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness.

AgentDosingNotable ADRs
BenralizumabSC every 4 weeks x3, then every 8 weeksHeadache, pyrexia, pharyngitis
MepolizumabSC every 4 weeksInjection-site reactions, headache, back pain, fatigue
ReslizumabIV every 4 weeksUS Boxed Warning for anaphylaxis; oropharyngeal pain, CPK elevation, myalgia, rare malignancies

Therapeutic use: add-on, maintenance therapy for severe asthma with an eosinophilic phenotype. Hypersensitivity reactions have occurred with all three drugs.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
What is the mechanism of omalizumab, and which asthma population is it indicated for?
AA humanized monoclonal antibody against IL-5, indicated for mild intermittent asthma
BA humanized monoclonal antibody directed against IgE that prevents binding to Fc receptors on mast cells/basophils, indicated for severe asthma with evidence of allergic sensitization
CA leukotriene receptor antagonist indicated for AERD only
DA PDE4 inhibitor indicated for COPD with chronic bronchitis
EA short-acting muscarinic antagonist indicated for acute bronchospasm
Explanation: Omalizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody directed against IgE. It binds IgE and prevents its binding to the high-affinity FcER1 and FcER2 receptors on mast cells, basophils, dendritic cells, and other inflammatory cells — blunting both the early and late allergic response. It is indicated for severe asthma with evidence of allergic sensitization, particularly in patients with a history of repeated exacerbations, high corticosteroid requirements, and poor pulmonary function.
Exam-style question
Omalizumab carries a US Boxed Warning for which adverse effect, and what is a notable feature of its timing?
AHepatotoxicity, which occurs only after 1 year of therapy
BQT prolongation, which occurs only with concomitant macrolide use
CBone marrow suppression, occurring exclusively within the first week
DAnaphylaxis (bronchospasm, hypotension, syncope, urticaria, and/or angioedema), which may occur as early as the first dose or as late as beyond one year of regularly administered therapy
EAdrenal insufficiency, occurring only after abrupt discontinuation
Explanation: Omalizumab carries a US Boxed Warning for anaphylaxis, which can present as bronchospasm, hypotension, syncope, urticaria, and/or angioedema of the throat or tongue. Notably, this reaction may occur as early as the first dose given or may occur unpredictably beyond one year of regularly administered therapy — patients require observation and preparedness for anaphylaxis at every dose, not just the first.
Exam-style question
Which class of biologic targets interleukin-5 (IL-5) or its receptor, and for what asthma phenotype is it used?
AAnti-IL-5 therapy (benralizumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab); used as add-on maintenance therapy for severe asthma with an eosinophilic phenotype
BAnti-IgE therapy (omalizumab); used for eosinophilic asthma
CPDE4 inhibitors; used for allergic asthma
DLeukotriene inhibitors; used for AERD only
EMuscarinic antagonists; used for COPD only
Explanation: Benralizumab, mepolizumab, and reslizumab are anti-IL-5 therapies (mepolizumab/reslizumab are humanized IL-5 monoclonal antibodies; benralizumab targets the IL-5 receptor). IL-5 is the major cytokine driving eosinophil growth, differentiation, recruitment, and activation, so these drugs inhibit eosinophilic inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness — used as add-on maintenance therapy specifically for severe asthma with an eosinophilic phenotype.
Exam-style question
Which anti-IL-5 agent carries a US Boxed Warning for anaphylaxis and is also associated with elevated creatine phosphokinase and rare malignancies?
AMepolizumab
BBenralizumab
CReslizumab
DOmalizumab
ERoflumilast
Explanation: Reslizumab carries a US Boxed Warning for anaphylaxis and may cause oropharyngeal pain, creatine phosphokinase elevations, myalgia, and rare malignancies. Benralizumab's more typical adverse effects are headache, pyrexia, and pharyngitis; mepolizumab's are injection-site reactions, headache, back pain, and fatigue.

Part 4 — Clinical Step Therapy

Classifying & treating asthma severity

Asthma severity assessment considers: reported symptoms over the previous 2-4 weeks, current lung function, and the number of exacerbations requiring oral glucocorticoids in the previous year. Patients are classified as:

CategoryRecommended step
IntermittentStep 1
Mild persistentStep 2
Moderate persistentStep 3
Severe persistentStep 4 or 5

Step 1 (intermittent): PRN SABA alone. Step 2 (preferred): daily low-dose ICS + PRN SABA, or PRN concomitant ICS and SABA. Step 3 (preferred): daily and PRN low-dose ICS-formoterol combination — the same inhaler serves as both scheduled maintenance and PRN reliever (single maintenance-and-reliever therapy). Step 4-5: escalating ICS-LABA doses ± LAMA, up to daily high-dose ICS-LABA + LAMA + PRN SABA (Step 5) or the addition of oral systemic corticosteroids and/or an asthma biologic (anti-IgE, anti-IL5, anti-IL5R, anti-IL4/IL13) at Step 6.

Clinical pearlGINA international guidelines diverge somewhat from the US NAEPP approach — most notably in recommending against SABA-only treatment at Step 1, instead favoring as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol from the very start to ensure every reliever dose also delivers anti-inflammatory therapy.

Assessing control & adjusting therapy

First check adherence, inhaler technique, environmental factors, and comorbid conditions. Step up if needed and reassess in 2-6 weeks. Step down if possible, once asthma has been well-controlled for at least 3 consecutive months. Consult an asthma specialist if Step 4 or higher is required. Control assessment involves both impairment and risk, using objective measures, self-reported control, and healthcare utilization.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
For a patient with mild persistent asthma (Step 2) being newly started on controller therapy, what is the preferred regimen under the 2020 NAEPP-focused updates?
ADaily high-dose ICS-LABA plus oral corticosteroids
BDaily LAMA monotherapy
CDaily oral theophylline alone
DOmalizumab as first-line monotherapy
EDaily low-dose ICS and PRN SABA, or PRN concomitant ICS and SABA
Explanation: For Step 2 (mild persistent asthma), the preferred regimen is daily low-dose ICS with PRN SABA, or PRN concomitant ICS and SABA. Intermittent asthma (Step 1) uses PRN SABA alone, while alternative Step 2 options include daily leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) plus PRN SABA, or cromolyn/nedocromil/zileuton/theophylline plus PRN SABA — all less preferred than ICS-based regimens.
Exam-style question
What distinguishes the preferred regimen at Step 3 (moderate persistent asthma) from Step 2, and what does "daily and PRN ICS-formoterol" specifically refer to as a strategy?
AStep 3 removes ICS entirely in favor of LAMA monotherapy
BStep 3 preferred therapy is daily and PRN low-dose ICS-formoterol combination — using the same ICS-formoterol inhaler both for daily maintenance and as the reliever for symptoms (a single-inhaler maintenance-and-reliever strategy)
CStep 3 is identical to Step 2 but with twice the SABA dose
DStep 3 replaces all inhaled therapy with oral prednisone
EStep 3 is defined solely by the addition of omalizumab
Explanation: At Step 3, the preferred regimen is daily and PRN low-dose ICS-formoterol combination therapy — the same combination inhaler is used both for scheduled daily maintenance dosing AND as the reliever whenever the patient has symptoms (single maintenance-and-reliever therapy, or SMART strategy), rather than using a separate SABA as the reliever.
Exam-style question
Once a patient's asthma has been well-controlled for at least 3 consecutive months, what is the recommended next step, and what should be checked before ANY step change (up or down)?
AImmediately discontinue all therapy; no further evaluation needed
BAutomatically step up therapy regardless of symptom control, to prevent future exacerbations
CSwitch directly to biologic therapy
DConsider stepping down therapy; before any step up or step down, first check adherence, inhaler technique, environmental factors, and comorbid conditions
ERefer to pulmonology only if stepping down, never if stepping up
Explanation: Asthma control should be reassessed and therapy stepped up if needed (typically reassessed in 2-6 weeks after a change) or stepped down if possible once the patient has been well-controlled for at least 3 consecutive months. Before any step change in either direction, adherence, inhaler technique, environmental factors, and comorbid conditions should be checked first, since these are common reasons for apparent treatment failure.

Classifying & treating COPD (GOLD approach)

Nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic COPD therapy are both guided by disease severity. The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) criteria categorize patients into Group A, B, or E based on symptom assessment and risk of future exacerbations/hospitalizations, which aligns to a recommended pharmacologic strategy.

Nonpharmacologic interventions (all patients)

Smoking cessation; reduction of other risk factors (e.g., open cooking fire exposure); vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19); regular physical activity; a short-acting bronchodilator as needed for acute dyspnea; regular review of correct inhaler technique; assessment of hypoxemia/hypercarbia for possible long-term oxygen and/or noninvasive ventilation.

GOLD group assignment

First ask: has the patient had 2 or more moderate exacerbations or at least 1 hospitalization for COPD exacerbation in the past year? If yes → Group E. If no, quantify dyspnea/symptoms with the mMRC scale and CAT score: mMRC <2 and CAT <10 → Group A; mMRC ≥2 or CAT ≥10 → Group B.

GroupPreferred pharmacologic strategy
Group ALAMA (tiotropium) + as-needed SABA (albuterol) (preferred); alternatively LABA (salmeterol, formoterol) + SAMA-SABA (ipratropium + albuterol) or SABA (albuterol) alone; or as-needed SAMA-SABA/SABA alone if only occasional minimal symptoms
Group BLAMA-LABA (tiotropium + salmeterol/formoterol) dual bronchodilator therapy + SABA (albuterol) as needed
Group E, eosinophils <300/microL and no hospitalizationLAMA-LABA (tiotropium + salmeterol/formoterol) dual bronchodilator therapy + SABA (albuterol) as needed
Group E, eosinophils ≥300/microL OR hospitalization for exacerbationICS-LAMA-LABA (budesonide/fluticasone + tiotropium + salmeterol/formoterol) (triple) therapy + SABA (albuterol) as needed
Clinical pearlGroup E splits into two very different regimens depending on eosinophil count/hospitalization history — this is the direct clinical application of the earlier fact that ICS benefit in COPD tracks with eosinophilia and exacerbation severity, not with airflow limitation alone.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
Which nonpharmacologic interventions are recommended for essentially all COPD patients regardless of GOLD group?
AOnly supplemental oxygen and nothing else
BSmoking cessation, reduction of other risk factors (e.g., open cooking fire exposure), influenza/pneumococcal/COVID-19 vaccination, regular physical activity, and pulmonary rehabilitation as indicated
CDaily systemic corticosteroids for every patient
DRoutine prophylactic antibiotics for all patients
EAvoidance of all bronchodilator therapy until Group E is reached
Explanation: Regardless of GOLD group, general and preventive care for all COPD patients includes smoking cessation counseling, reduction of other risk factor exposure (e.g., biomass/open cooking fire smoke), vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19), regular physical activity, a short-acting bronchodilator as needed for acute dyspnea, review of correct inhaler technique, and assessment for hypoxemia/hypercarbia to determine need for long-term oxygen or noninvasive ventilation.
Exam-style question
In the GOLD approach to COPD, what determines whether a newly diagnosed patient is placed in Group A, Group B, or Group E?
AGroup is determined by exacerbation history (2+ moderate exacerbations or 1+ hospitalization → Group E) and, if not, by symptom burden via mMRC/CAT scores (higher symptoms → Group B, lower → Group A)
BGroup is determined solely by FEV1 percent predicted, with no role for symptoms or exacerbation history
CAll COPD patients start in Group A regardless of any clinical feature
DGroup assignment is based only on smoking pack-years
EGroup E is reserved for patients already on triple inhaled therapy
Explanation: GOLD group assignment starts by asking whether the patient has had 2 or more moderate exacerbations, or at least 1 hospitalization for a COPD exacerbation, in the past year — if yes, the patient is Group E regardless of symptom scores. If no, symptom burden is quantified with the mMRC dyspnea scale and CAT score: mMRC <2 and CAT <10 defines Group A (lower symptom burden), while mMRC ≥2 or CAT ≥10 defines Group B (higher symptom burden).
Exam-style question
What is the preferred initial pharmacologic therapy for a newly diagnosed GOLD Group A COPD patient?
AICS-LAMA-LABA triple therapy
BDaily oral roflumilast
CA LAMA plus as-needed SABA (preferred), or alternatively LABA plus SAMA-SABA or SABA alone, or as-needed SABA/SAMA-SABA alone if only occasional minimal symptoms
DOmalizumab
EDaily oral prednisone taper
Explanation: GOLD Group A (low exacerbation risk, low symptom burden) is preferentially managed with a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) plus an as-needed SABA for acute dyspnea, with LABA plus SAMA-SABA or SABA alone as alternatives; patients with only occasional, minimal symptoms may be managed with an as-needed short-acting bronchodilator alone rather than scheduled long-acting therapy.
Exam-style question
A newly diagnosed GOLD Group E COPD patient (frequent exacerbator) with a peripheral eosinophil count of 450/microL should be started on which regimen?
ALAMA plus as-needed SABA alone
BLAMA-LABA dual bronchodilator therapy with SABA as needed
CRoflumilast monotherapy
DOmalizumab plus SABA
EICS-LAMA-LABA (triple) therapy with SABA as needed for acute dyspnea
Explanation: In GOLD Group E, if the patient has high peripheral eosinophil levels (≥300/microL) or has required hospitalization for a COPD exacerbation, ICS-LAMA-LABA triple therapy is recommended (plus SABA as needed for acute dyspnea). Group E patients without high eosinophils/hospitalization instead receive LAMA-LABA dual bronchodilator therapy without the inhaled steroid, since ICS benefit in COPD tracks with eosinophil count and exacerbation severity.

Part 5 — Comparing Asthma & COPD Pharmacotherapy

Asthma vs. COPD: pharmacologic strategy compared

FeatureAsthmaCOPD
Underlying inflammationEosinophilic / Th2-driven (IgE, mast cells, eosinophils)More neutrophilic; some overlap with eosinophilic phenotype
Corticosteroid roleFoundational — reduces symptoms, hyperreactivity, exacerbations; started once SABA use > 2x/weekDoes not alter progression/mortality; reserved for severe disease + frequent exacerbations (esp. with eosinophilia)
LABA monotherapyContraindicated — US Boxed Warning; must pair with ICSAccepted as part of LAMA-LABA dual bronchodilator therapy
First-line maintenance bronchodilatorNot first-line; ICS is foundational, with SABA as relieverLAMA is preferred first-line agent (Group A)
Step-based frameworkNAEPP/GINA Steps 1-6, based on symptom/exacerbation-based severity classificationGOLD Groups A/B/E, based on exacerbation history + symptom burden (mMRC/CAT)
Biologic (monoclonal antibody) therapyOmalizumab (anti-IgE), anti-IL5 agents — reserved for severe, refractory disease with an allergic or eosinophilic phenotypeNo FDA-approved role for these biologics in COPD in this framework
Leukotriene inhibitorsAdd-on maintenance therapy; specific role in AERDNo role
PDE4 inhibitor (roflumilast)No roleSevere disease, frequent exacerbations, chronic bronchitis
Clinical pearlIf you remember only one thing from this comparison table: corticosteroids and LABA monotherapy behave almost oppositely in the two diseases. ICS is central to asthma but narrowly indicated in COPD; LABA monotherapy is forbidden in asthma but standard in COPD. Exam questions love to test exactly this asymmetry.

Check yourself

Exam-style question
Comparing corticosteroid use in asthma versus COPD, which statement is most accurate?
ACorticosteroids work identically in both diseases and are first-line in both
BICS have no role at all in COPD under any circumstance
CICS are contraindicated in asthma but first-line in COPD
DIn asthma, ICS reduce exacerbations, improve symptoms and airway caliber, and are recommended broadly based on SABA use frequency; in COPD, ICS do not alter disease progression/mortality and are reserved for severe disease with frequent exacerbations (particularly with eosinophilia)
EOral corticosteroids are used chronically as maintenance therapy in both diseases
Explanation: This distinction is a favorite exam point: in asthma, inhaled corticosteroids are foundational, broadly recommended once SABA use exceeds twice weekly, and clearly improve symptoms, airway hyperreactivity, and exacerbation frequency. In COPD, by contrast, ICS do not meaningfully change disease progression or mortality and are reserved for a specific subgroup — severe disease (FEV1 <50%) with frequent exacerbations, especially with elevated eosinophils — reflecting a different underlying inflammatory biology (eosinophilic/Th2 in asthma vs. more neutrophilic in COPD).
Exam-style question
Comparing the role of LABA monotherapy in asthma versus COPD, which is correct?
ALABA monotherapy carries a US Boxed Warning against use in asthma (must be paired with ICS) but is an accepted component of COPD bronchodilator therapy (e.g., within LAMA-LABA regimens)
BLABA monotherapy is safe and preferred first-line in both diseases
CLABA monotherapy is banned in both asthma and COPD
DLABA monotherapy is preferred in asthma but banned in COPD
EThere is no meaningful difference in LABA safety between the two diseases
Explanation: LABAs must never be used as monotherapy in asthma because of the boxed-warning risk of increased asthma-related death (SMART study) — they must be combined with an ICS. In COPD, however, LABAs (often paired with a LAMA, as in LAMA-LABA dual bronchodilator therapy) are an accepted, guideline-recommended component of stepwise management without that same monotherapy restriction.
